# Filtering by file type in ripgrep

If you search text for a living, you already reach for globs (`-g '*.rs'`)
to narrow a search to one kind of file. ripgrep's file-type flags do the
same job, but with a name instead of a pattern to remember and retype.
This guide covers the four flags that make up that system: `--type`/`-t`,
`--type-not`/`-T`, `--type-add`, and `--type-list`.

## The basic idea: `--type`/`-t`

`--type` limits ripgrep to files matching a named type. A type is just a
name bound to one or more globs. Instead of writing:

```
$ rg 'int main' -g '*.{c,h}'
```

you write:

```
$ rg 'int main' -tc
```

or the longer form:

```
$ rg 'int main' --type c
```

`-t` and its type name can be run together (`-trust`) or passed as separate
arguments (`-t rust`, `--type rust`). You can pass `--type` more than once;
each one adds another type to search, so `rg foo -tc -tcpp` searches both C
and C++ files.

Note that `--type` has *lower precedence* than both `-g`/`--glob` and any
rules found in your ignore files. A `.gitignore` entry or an explicit
`-g '!*.rs'` can still exclude a file even if it matches a type you've
selected.

## Excluding a type: `--type-not`/`-T`

`--type-not` is the mirror image: `-t` means "include files of this
type," `-T` means "exclude files of this type."

```
$ rg clap --type-not rust
$ rg clap -Trust
```

Like `--type`, `--type-not` can be repeated, and `-t`/`-T` flags can be
mixed in one invocation — `-Trust -ttoml -Tjson` excludes Rust and JSON
while including TOML.

## Listing what's available: `--type-list`

Before filtering by a type, it helps to know what it actually matches.
`--type-list` prints every supported type, one per line, as a name
followed by a colon and a comma-separated list of its globs:

```
$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:'
make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
```

ripgrep ships with a large set of predefined types covering well-known
public formats — things like `rust`, `py`/`python`, `markdown`/`md`, `c`,
`cpp`, and `go` (run `--type-list` with no other arguments for the full,
current set). `--type-list` also takes into account any `--type-add` or
`--type-clear` flags on the same command line, so it reflects the types
actually in effect for that invocation, not just the built-in defaults.

## Defining your own types: `--type-add`

If none of the built-in types fit, `--type-add` lets you define one. It
takes a single `name:glob` pair, and only one glob per flag — pass
`--type-add` multiple times (or use brace expansion) to add several globs
to the same name:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title
```

This defines a `web` type matching HTML, CSS, and JS files, then searches
it for `title`. Unless you've used `--type-clear` (below), globs added
with `--type-add`
go *on top of* any existing globs for that name — including built-in
types. So `--type-add 'rust:*.rspec'` extends, rather than replaces, the
existing `rust` type.

`--type-add` also supports an `include:` directive, letting a new type
pull in the rules of other already-defined types by name:

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' --type-add 'src:*.foo'
```

This defines `src` as everything matched by the `cpp`, `py`, and `md`
types, plus `*.foo` — additional `--type-add` flags keep extending it.
Type names may only contain Unicode letters and numbers, no punctuation.

**`--type-add` is not persistent.** It only affects the invocation it's
passed to; ripgrep does not remember custom types between runs. To make a
custom type available every time, either alias the flag into your shell
(`alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"`) or add
`--type-add=web:*.{html,css,js}` as a line in your ripgrep configuration
file (set via the `RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH` environment variable), which
ripgrep prepends to every invocation's arguments.

A related flag, `--type-clear TYPE`, removes the globs previously defined
for a type name — including built-in ones — without removing the name
itself, so you can redefine it from scratch. Like `--type-add`, it must be
passed on every invocation.

## The special `all` type

Both `--type` and `--type-not` accept the special value `all`, which
behaves as if you'd passed the flag once for every type ripgrep knows
about, including any you defined with `--type-add`.

- `--type all` (equivalent to `-t agda -t asciidoc -t asm ...` for every
  known type) puts ripgrep into "whitelist" mode: it searches only files
  it recognizes via *some* type definition.
- `--type-not all` puts it into "blacklist" mode: it searches only files
  that *don't* match any known type.

This distinction matters for files without a telltale extension. Given an
extension-less shell script `my-shell-script` that sources a library
`my-shell-library.bash`, both `rg --type sh` and `rg --type all` search
only `my-shell-library.bash` — the `sh` type's globs require an extension.
`rg --type-not all` does the reverse: it searches `my-shell-script`
(unrecognized by any type) but skips `my-shell-library.bash`.

## Putting it together

A typical workflow: run `rg --type-list` once to check a type's globs or
confirm a name exists, reach for `-t`/`-T` in day-to-day searches, and fall
back to `--type-add` (aliased or in your config file) for a recurring
search over files that don't map onto a built-in type. For one-off or
highly specific filename patterns, `-g`/`--glob` still wins on precedence
and needs no type definition — the two mechanisms complement each other.
